drafted.title: Unvalidated tool-call and inference input parameters
drafted.description: Agent frameworks, MCP servers, and model-serving endpoints accept attacker-influenced tool-call arguments, API fields, or inference payloads (file paths, parameter names, tensor shapes, provider configs) and pass them into sensitive operations—command execution, file access, memory allocation, protocol parsing—without adequate type, bound, or allow-list checks. Because the trust boundary sits at the agent's tool/protocol interface rather than deep in business logic, a single crafted input can trigger remote code execution, path traversal, SSRF, or denial of service across the whole agent pipeline.

drafted.title: Unrestricted external entity resolution in agent XML/document parsers
drafted.description: An agent tool or an embedded third-party library parses attacker-supplied XML (documents, SAML/SOAP messages, SVG/office files, config or BOM uploads) without disabling DTD processing and external entity resolution, so a crafted DOCTYPE causes the parser to read arbitrary local files or issue outbound requests (SSRF) and return the results to the attacker. Because the flaw typically lives in a reused parsing dependency rather than agent-specific code, any agent that ingests or transforms untrusted XML-based content through such a tool inherits the vulnerability, enabling data exfiltration, credential theft, internal network probing, or denial of service via entity-expansion bombs.

drafted.title: Downstream interpreter injection via unneutralized agent-generated output
drafted.description: Agent frameworks and MCP tool servers build shell commands, SQL/Cypher queries, templates, log entries, or config manifests by directly concatenating LLM-generated text or externally-sourced content (crawled pages, tool arguments, filenames) without neutralizing special elements like quotes, backticks, newlines, or template delimiters. An attacker who can influence that content — via prompt injection, a malicious file/URL the agent processes, or crafted tool input — breaks out of the intended data context to achieve remote code execution, query/record manipulation, privilege escalation, or forged log/context entries, and because the agent executes autonomously this typically requires no further human approval step.

drafted.title: Open redirect to attacker-controlled host via unvalidated URL parameter
drafted.description: An agent-facing web service (login/logout flow, OAuth or SAML redirect_uri, MCP registry/OAuth client-registration endpoint, or a tool parameter) builds an HTTP redirect or absolute link from attacker-supplied input (query string, Host header, or form field) without validating it against an allowlist of trusted destinations. Attackers abuse the trusted domain to redirect a victim's browser, an authenticating agent, or a follow-on HTTP client to an attacker-controlled host, enabling phishing, theft of OAuth authorization codes/session tokens, or coercing an autonomous agent into exfiltrating data or credentials to an external endpoint it believed was part of its own trust chain.

drafted.title: Cross-origin MCP tool invocation via missing Origin/Host validation
drafted.description: MCP servers exposing local HTTP/SSE transports frequently omit or incorrectly implement validation of the Origin/Host header (e.g. empty-string defaults, prefix-match bypasses, or no check at all), so a malicious web page loaded in the victim's browser can send cross-origin requests — or use DNS rebinding to defeat same-origin assumptions — directly to the loopback-bound MCP endpoint. Because the server trusts any request that reaches its socket, the attacker's page can silently invoke tools, read resources, or complete OAuth-backed flows as the logged-in agent, achieving unauthenticated remote tool execution without ever touching the agent's actual authentication layer.

drafted.title: Path traversal via unsanitized file paths in agent tool/plugin endpoints
drafted.description: An agent-adjacent web service exposes file-handling endpoints (plugin/extension install, model download, settings backup, log/audio retrieval) that build filesystem paths from user- or tool-supplied input without canonicalizing absolute paths or OS-specific '..' and backslash sequences, letting an attacker escape the intended directory to read, overwrite, or drop arbitrary files. Because these endpoints often back the agent's plugin/extension installation or model-loading pipeline, the resulting arbitrary file write frequently escalates to remote code execution when the planted file is later loaded or executed by the agent runtime.

drafted.title: Unsafe eval of untrusted input in agent workflow/tool expression engines
drafted.description: Agent and workflow-orchestration platforms (low-code builders, expression evaluators, tool-call parsers, custom-component executors) pass attacker-influenced strings — prompt content, tool-call arguments, workflow expressions, YAML/SCXML fields, or user-supplied node code — into eval()/exec()-style dynamic evaluators or weakly isolated sandboxes. Because the evaluator interprets this data as executable code rather than inert data, an attacker can break out of the intended expression language and achieve arbitrary code execution on the host running the agent.

drafted.title: Arbitrary file read/write via relative path traversal in tool filename parameters
drafted.description: Agent and MCP-adjacent tool endpoints (file uploads, workflow save/load, profile pictures, personality/plugin folders, artifact stores, media references) accept a model- or user-supplied filename or path and use it to build a filesystem path without canonicalizing and rejecting '../' sequences or symlink tricks, letting an attacker escape the intended storage directory. This allows arbitrary file read or write on the host, which can leak credentials/config, overwrite application code or plugins, or plant files that are later loaded and executed by the agent runtime.

drafted.title: Unrestricted dangerous file upload leading to remote code execution in agent file-handling endpoints
drafted.description: Agent-adjacent platforms (chatbot UIs, vector databases, ML/training tools, attachment or 'send file to AI' endpoints) accept user-supplied files without validating true type, extension, or content, letting an attacker upload a web shell, script, or archive into a web-reachable or interpreter-reachable path. When that file is later served or invoked, it executes with the host process's privileges, giving the attacker full code execution on the system hosting the agent or its tools.

drafted.title: Evade incomplete denylist validators via alternate syntax, encoding, or type confusion
drafted.description: Agent platforms and MCP servers often gate dangerous tool actions (shell execution, code/SQL validators, deserialization, command approval prompts, env var controls) behind a denylist of known-bad tokens or patterns rather than an allowlist; because such lists can never enumerate every syntactic variant, attackers craft logically-equivalent but textually-unlisted inputs (parameter expansion, homoglyphs, alternate module/class paths, nested env-var tricks, polymorphic subtype arrays) that slip past the filter while still triggering the forbidden behavior. The result is that a guardrail believed to block RCE, SSRF, command injection, or unsafe deserialization is silently bypassed, letting an agent or connected tool execute attacker-controlled code or requests with the same privileges as if no check existed.
